say: You give it a solid and its measurements. It gives back the **volume**, the space inside.
The key idea: every solid has a formula on the tables. Pick the one for your solid, then substitute carefully.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside Paper 2 questions on cones, cylinders and spheres (a part or two most years, often 5 to 15 marks), and sometimes with a formula given in a Paper 1 question.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it almost every year, mostly as a part of its own on Paper 2 (sphere, cylinder, cone, 5 to 10 marks), and often again when two volumes are subtracted.

example.question: A solid cone has base radius $6$ cm and vertical height $8$ cm. Find its volume, correct to the nearest $\text{cm}^3$.

steps.title: Pick the formula
steps.say: Name the solid and write its formula. For a cone, $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Then pick out the radius $\hl{1}{r}$ and the height $\hl{2}{h}$ from the question.

lines.text: The radius is the base radius. The height is the vertical height, not the slant.

steps.title: Substitute the numbers
steps.say: Put $\hl{1}{6}$ in for $r$ and $\hl{2}{8}$ in for $h$. Square the radius first.

steps.title: Round the answer
steps.say: The question wants the nearest $\text{cm}^3$, so put $\pi$ into the calculator and round.

say: You give it a radius and an angle. It gives back the **arc length** and the **sector area**.
The key idea: a sector is a fraction of a circle. The angle over $360^\circ$ is that fraction, and it multiplies the circumference or the area.

how.higher: Higher level uses it almost every year as a step inside Paper 2 questions on circles, cones made from sectors and segments (usually 5 to 10 marks), and once in radians on Paper 1.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it nearly every year, mostly as a part of its own on Paper 2, such as the area between two sectors or the length of a curved edge.

example.question: A sector of a circle has radius $9$ cm and angle $80^\circ$. Find the length of its arc and the area of the sector, in terms of $\pi$.

steps.title: Find the fraction of the circle
steps.say: The sector is part of a full circle. Its angle over $360^\circ$ gives the fraction.

steps.title: Find the arc length
steps.say: The arc is that fraction of the circumference, $2\pi r$.

steps.title: Find the sector area
steps.say: The area is the same fraction of the full circle, $\pi r^2$.

say: You give it a solid and its measurements. It gives back the **surface area**, the area of the outside.
The key idea: find the area of each face or curved part, then add them. A cone needs its **slant** height, which you get from Pythagoras.

how.higher: Higher level uses it rarely, as a step inside Paper 2 cone questions (three parts in eleven years), usually after finding the slant height.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it most years, usually as a part of its own on Paper 1 or Paper 2 (cylinder, cone, sphere or a block), often worth 5 to 10 marks.

example.question: A cone has base radius $5$ cm and vertical height $12$ cm. Find its curved surface area, in terms of $\pi$, and to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the slant height
steps.say: The curved surface needs the slant height $\hl{1}{l}$, not the vertical height. The radius, height and slant make a right-angled triangle, so use Pythagoras.

steps.title: Use the curved area formula
steps.say: The curved surface area of a cone is $\pi r l$. Put in $r = 5$ and $l = \hl{1}{13}$.

higher.tip: For a cone, find the slant height with Pythagoras first. It earns marks on its own.

say: You give it a strip width and a list of heights. It gives back an **estimate** of the area under a curved edge.
The key idea: split the area into strips of equal width. The first and last heights count once. Every height between counts twice.

how.higher: Higher level used it once, in 2015 on Paper 1, as a table and an area estimate followed by the percentage error.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it in five of eleven years, as a part of its own on Paper 1 or Paper 2, worth 5 to 10 marks.

example.question: A garden is $16$ m long. Its width is measured every $4$ m along the length: $6$, $9$, $11$, $8$ and $5$ metres. Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the garden.

steps.title: Find the strip width
steps.say: The widths are the heights $y$. The strip width $\hl{1}{h}$ is the gap between them.

lines.text: There are five heights and four strips.

steps.title: Add the ends and the middles
steps.say: The rule adds the first and last heights once. It adds every height in between twice.
